title: Annex G
text:
## Annex G

#### Foreign trade

This annex provides an overview of published HMRC trade data on energy products. There are some inconsistencies between this data and that presented in the main chapters of DUKES. In the main chapters, the trade data are produced from a combination of data from HMRC and from companies responding to DECC statistical surveys. In particular there are significant differences in the data for petroleum products. These data are presented for users who use energy trade data alongside trade data for other products.

Main points for 2013

Provisional data from HMRC show that: 
 There were a total of 164 million tonnes of oil equivalent (mtoe) imported to the UK in 2013, 
marginally down on 2012 levels, but at a near record high. 
 Exports fell by 3.8 per cent to 85.4 mtoe, and have fallen by a third in the last 10 years. 
 The energy trade deficit stood at £18.3 billion, 17 per cent lower than in 2012. The fall was due to a 
reduced deficit in crude oil and petroleum products which at £5.7 billion was 46 per cent lower than 
in 2012. DECC analysis utilising company data suggests that this fall in the deficit may be 
overstated. 
Imports by fuel type: 
 Coal imports increased by 7.4 per cent to 46 million tonnes, with growth in both steam coal mainly 
used for electricity generation and coking coal mainly within the iron and steel industry. 
 Crude oil imports fell by 12 per cent to 48.9 million tonnes largely due to lower demand from 
refineries. 
 Despite HMRC trade data showing the UK being a net exporter of petroleum products, net exports 
in 2013 fell by more than half due in the main to the closure of the Coryton refinery. DECC’s 
analysis using company data indicates the UK was a net importer of product in 2013. 
 Gas imports fell by 2 per cent to 525 GWh, within which there was a sharp fall in LNG imports from 
Qatar. 

Introduction

G.1 This annex provides an overview of the UK energy trade commodities which also corresponds with 
that published in the Overseas Trade Statistics of the United Kingdom (O.T.S.) 1. Section I of this annex 
covers energy trade volume while section II covers energy trade value. 
G.2 The volume information in section I, focuses on the declaration made to HM Revenue and Customs 
(HMRC) on UK imports and exports in relation to countries outside the European Union (EU) as well as 
on arrivals and dispatches in relation to EU member states. In table G.1, DECC has converted the 
HMRC data into mtoe, so that energy sources can be combined to provide an overview of total trade. 
The value information, in section II, corresponds to that published by the Office for National Statistics 
energy trade value data. 
G.3 In this annex, DECC has used estimates based on its industry trade reports, for some recent gas 
data, to improve on the accuracy and quality of the data, in which case those estimates are clearly 
indicated and footnoted in the tables. The latest data for 2013 are provisional. 

SECTION I - Volume

1.1 Overview - Import and export of fuels

G.4 In the 1970s the UK was a net importer of energy. Discoveries of oil and gas from the North Sea and the price spikes of 1973 led to a large rise in domestic UK crude oil production. In the early 1980s the UK became a net exporter of energy. However, as a result of the Piper Alpha disaster in 1988, oil production fell, leading to the UK reverting back to become a net importer of energy. The UK once again became a net exporter in the mid-1990s as a result of growth in the North Sea production, but after the peak in 1999, North Sea production has continued to slow down and in 2004 the UK once again became a net importer of fuels. Chart G.1a below shows the UK net import dependence level from 1970 to 2013, based on DECC data. In 2013, the dependency level (net imports compared to demand) increased to 47.1 per cent, its highest level since 1974.

Chart G.1a - UK import dependency, 1970 to 2013

Source: DECC G.5 HMRC data shows that since the switch from being a net exporter in 2003 to a net importer in 2004, the UK has continued to remain a net importer of energy. Net imports have grown considerably in the past few years as the falls in UK energy consumption have been outweighed by the continuing decline in production. In 2013, total net imports of fuels stood at 78.6 million tonnes of oil equivalent (mtoe); 3.3 mtoe lower than in 2012, as both imports and exports fell by 4.0 per cent (Chart G.1b). Table G.1, at the end of this annex, provides the UK import and export quantities for all fuel types since 2001.

Chart G.1b - UK net imports of fuel, 2001 to 2013p

G.6 Chart G.2 illustrates the trade by fuel type in 2013 with the UK a net importer of all fuels except for petroleum products. However net exports of petroleum products has been on the decline since 2010 and in 2013 it fell further to 2.5 mtoe due to the temporary closures of two major refineries. Additionally the closure of the Coryton refinery in July 2012 has also had an impact on production. In 2013, imports of petroleum products increased slightly by 2.6 per cent to 33.6 mtoe.

Chart G.2 - Imports and exports by fuel type, 2013

1.2 Coal and manufactured solid fuels

G.7 Imports of coal had been on the decline since its peak in 2006, but in recent years, increases in gas prices has resulted in more coal being used to satisfy demand from electricity generators and thus higher imports. Chart G.3 illustrates the trends in the imports of coal by country for the years 2001-2013. In 2013, the UK imported 46.0 million tonnes of coal and other solid fuels, an increase of 7.4 per cent (3.2 million tonnes) on the previous year. G.8 Table G.2, at the end of this annex, provides a breakdown of HMRC imports and exports of steam coal, coking coal, anthracite and other solid fuels by country of origin and destination.

Chart G.3: Imports of coal by country of origin 2001 to 2013

G.9 Coal imports from Russia have been steadily increasing and in 2005, Russia overtook South Africa 
to become the UK’s largest coal provider and has since continued to be so. In 2013, 38.8 per cent of the 
UK’s coal imports were from Russia followed by 26.4 per cent from the US and a further 18.8 per cent 
from Colombia. 
G.10 Of the total coal imported in 2013, 85.1 per cent was steam coal, 13.8 per cent coking coal and the 
rest anthracite and other solid fuels. Whilst the import of steam coal from Russia increased by 3.5 per 
cent to 16.8 million tonnes and from the US by 19 per cent to 9.3 million tonnes; imports from Colombia 
fell by 5.5 per cent to 8.6 million tonnes. 
G.11 In 2013, 43.7 per cent of the UK coking coal imports came from the US followed by 23.4 per cent 
from Australia and 17.1 per cent from Russia. The bulk of anthracite and other solid fuels imports were 
from EU countries. 
G.12 Exports of coal and other solid fuels increased by 8.6 per cent to just over 1 million tonnes in 2013, 
with 42.5 per cent of exports to the Irish Republic. 
1.3 Crude oil and petroleum products 
G.13 Trade quantities, in thousands of tonnes, of crude oil and refined petroleum products are shown in 
in Table G.3. In the table, the import values per tonne are expressed on a cost, insurance and freight 
(c.i.f) basis while the export values are on a free on board (f.o.b) basis (e.g costs of goods to the 
purchaser abroad) – see section II for more details. 
G.14 Table G.4 provides trade data in crude oil by country where the import data, as far as possible, are 
on a ‘country of origin’ (or production) basis. Since becoming a net importer of crude oil in 2005, the UK’s 
net import of crude oil has steadily increased, rising significantly between 2010 and 2012. However in 
2013, net imports of crude oil, as reported by HMRC, fell back by 38 per cent to 13.3 million tonnes 
(chart G.4), driven by a sharp fall from Norway. 

Chart G.4 - Net trade of crude oil and petroleum products 2001 to 2013p

G.15 Norway remains the major crude oil supplier to the UK despite the continuous drop in imports from that country in the past few years (chart G.5). In 2013, Norway supplied around 41.5 per cent of the UK’s total crude oil imports compared to 50.2 per cent in 2012. The majority of the remaining imports came from the OPEC African countries such as Algeria, Angola, Libya and Nigeria which together accounted for 30.7 per cent of the total crude imports. Imports from Russia were 7.3 per cent of the total and from the Middle East, mainly from Saudi Arabia, 4.4 per cent, up from the 1.4 per cent share in 2012. In 2013, 77 per cent of the UK’s total exports of crude oil went to EU countries, broadly the same amount as in the past two years. The UK’s two largest markets in the EU are Germany and the Netherlands; the bulk of the exports to Germany are for refining and consumption, whilst exports to the Netherlands include oil destined for onward trade to other countries. Most of the non-EU exports of crude oil were to South Korea and the US.

Chart G.5 - Imports of crude oil by country of origin, 2001 to 2013p

G.16 The main refined petroleum products imported into the United Kingdom in 2013 were gas oil & diesel oil which together accounted for 38.5 per cent of the total; followed by aviation turbine fuel (kerosene) 26.0 per cent. The main refined petroleum products exported in 2013 were motor & aviation spirits; gas oil & diesel oil and fuel oils which together accounted for 73.5 per cent of the total. G.17 On a net trade basis in 2013, HMRC data show that the UK remained a net exporter of petroleum products with net exports of 1.5 million tonnes, the lowest since 2008 (chart G.4). In 2013 the UK was a net importer of aviation turbine fuel (6.9 million tonnes) and of diesel (4.0 million tonnes). The UK is a net exporter of petrol (6.1 million tonnes) and fuel oil 4.1 million tonnes.

1.4 Imports and exports of natural gas

G.18 Between 1997 and 2003 the UK was a net exporter of gas. UK gas production peaked in 2000 and 
has since been in general decline. As a result the UK has sought to access additional supplies of gas 
from a range of sources to bridge the gap between indigenous production and demand as reserves on 
the UK Continental Shelf deplete. 
G.19 Since 1999 natural gas imports have been increasing sharply, reaching a high to date in 2010. It 
has since been on the decline but at a slow rate. Equally over the past few years, natural gas exports 
have also been slowly declining. Chart G.6 depicts the trends in natural gas imports and exports by 
country. It also includes trends in the volume of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) imports (see Chart G.7 for 
country breakdown of LNG imports). The UK does not export LNG however it has one of the world’s 
largest importation terminals by capacity and the largest in Europe at the Isle of Grain, and the pipeline 
structure to export natural gas to the continent. 
G.20 Table G.5 gives a breakdown of imports and exports of natural gas by country of origin and 
destination. The data in the table are physical flows as reported by the pipeline or terminal operators to 
DECC. Whilst the data presented in the table differ from the nominated flows reported in Chapter 4, the 
overall net flows (e.g net imports or net exports) are essentially the same. 
G.21 In 2013 the UK exported 100 TWh of gas, a decrease of 24 per cent on 2012. The Republic of 
Ireland was the main destination of UK gas exports followed by Belgium. The other main destination of 
UK gas exports were the Netherlands, from the UK or UK share gas fields using the Dutch WGT pipeline 
system to Den Helder and Uithuizen. 

Chart G.6 - Imports and exports of natural gas by country, 2001 to 2013

G.22 In 2013 the UK imported 525 TWh of gas, 2 per cent less than in 2012, with 58 per cent of gas
